statement:
(i) Express $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}-\sqrt{3}}$ in the form $a\sqrt{5}+b\sqrt{3}$ where $a$ and $b$ are rational.

(ii) Show that $(\sqrt{5}-\sqrt{3})^2+(\sqrt{5}+\sqrt{3})^2=16$.
solution:
(i) Multiply numerator and denominator by $\sqrt{5}+\sqrt{3}$:
$$\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}-\sqrt{3}}=\frac{\sqrt{5}+\sqrt{3}}{(\sqrt{5})^2-(\sqrt{3})^2}=\frac{\sqrt{5}+\sqrt{3}}{5-3}=\frac{\sqrt{5}+\sqrt{3}}{2}=\tfrac12\sqrt{5}+\tfrac12\sqrt{3}.$$
So $a=\tfrac12$ and $b=\tfrac12$.

(ii) Expanding,
$$(\sqrt{5}-\sqrt{3})^2=5+3-2\sqrt{15}=8-2\sqrt{15},\qquad (\sqrt{5}+\sqrt{3})^2=8+2\sqrt{15}.$$
Adding gives $16$.
hints: For (i) rationalise using the conjugate sqrt(5)+sqrt(3).
For (ii) expand each square and add.
